content: Meningococcal disease is a severe illness caused by a type of bacteria. It is one of the leading causes of bacterial meningitis in children aged 2 to 18 years in the United States. Meningitis refers to an infection of the fluid surrounding the brain and spinal cord. Additionally, meningococcal disease can lead to bloodstream infections. Despite treatment with antibiotics, 10-15% of individuals with this disease die. Among those who survive, 11-19% may experience severe complications, such as limb loss, deafness, neurological problems, intellectual disabilities, seizures, or strokes. While anyone can contract meningococcal disease, it is most common in infants under one year of age and individuals with specific medical conditions, such as those without a functioning spleen. College freshmen living in dormitories are also at an increased risk. Although meningococcal infections can be treated with antibiotics like penicillin, approximately 1 in 10 people who contract the disease still die, and many survivors face lifelong consequences. This underscores the importance of prevention through vaccination, particularly for those at higher risk. Two types of meningococcal vaccines are available: the meningococcal polysaccharide vaccine (MPSV4), introduced in the 1970s, and the meningococcal conjugate vaccine (MCV4), licensed in 2005. Both vaccines protect against four types of meningococcal disease, including two of the three most common types in the United States and one type responsible for epidemics in Africa. While these vaccines do not prevent all forms of meningococcal disease, they are highly effective, protecting about 90% of vaccinated individuals. MCV4 is expected to provide better and longer-lasting protection and may also reduce the spread of the disease from person to person. MCV4 is recommended for all children during their routine preadolescent visit, typically at 11-12 years of age. For those who have not previously received MCV4, a dose is recommended at high school entry. Adolescents who wish to reduce their risk of meningococcal disease can also receive the vaccine. Additionally, meningococcal vaccination is recommended for individuals at increased risk, including: College freshmen living in dormitories. Microbiologists routinely exposed to meningococcal bacteria. Military recruits. Individuals traveling to or living in areas where meningococcal disease is common, such as parts of Africa. Individuals with a damaged or removed spleen. Individuals with terminal complement component deficiency, an immune system disorder. People exposed to meningitis during an outbreak. For individuals aged 11-55 in these risk groups, MCV4 is the preferred vaccine, but MPSV4 can be used if MCV4 is unavailable. MPSV4 is recommended for children aged 2-10 and adults over 55 who are at risk. People aged 2 years and older should receive one dose, though additional doses may be recommended for those at continued high risk. In special circumstances, MPSV4 may be recommended for children aged 3 months to 2 years, who should receive two doses three months apart. Certain individuals should not receive the meningococcal vaccine or should delay vaccination. These include: Anyone who has had a severe allergic reaction to a previous dose of meningococcal vaccine or any vaccine component. Anyone who is moderately or severely ill at the time of vaccination should wait until they recover. Those with mild illnesses can usually be vaccinated. Anyone with a history of Guillain-Barré Syndrome should consult their doctor before receiving MCV4. Pregnant women may receive meningococcal vaccines, but MCV4 has not been studied as extensively in pregnant women as MPSV4. It should only be used if clearly needed. Meningococcal vaccines can be administered alongside other vaccines. As with any medicine, vaccines can potentially cause serious problems, such as severe allergic reactions, though the risk of serious harm or death from the meningococcal vaccine is extremely small. Mild side effects, such as redness or pain at the injection site, occur in up to half of those vaccinated and typically last 1-2 days. These side effects are more common with MCV4 than MPSV4. A small percentage of individuals may develop a fever. Severe allergic reactions are very rare, occurring within minutes to hours of vaccination. A rare nervous system disorder called Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS) has been reported in some individuals who received MCV4, though it is unclear if the vaccine is a contributing factor. Even if it is, the risk is extremely small. If a moderate or severe reaction occurs, such as a high fever, behavioral changes, or signs of a serious allergic reaction (e.g., difficulty breathing, hoarseness, wheezing, hives, paleness, weakness, rapid heartbeat, or dizziness), seek medical attention immediately. Inform the doctor about the reaction, including the date and time it occurred and when the vaccine was administered. You can also report the reaction to the Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS) by calling 1-800-822-7967 or visiting their website. In rare cases of serious vaccine-related harm, the National Vaccine Injury Compensation Program (VICP) can help cover medical costs. For more information, call 1-800-338-2382 or visit the program's website. For additional information, consult your doctor or healthcare provider, contact your local or state health department's immunization program, or reach out to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) at 1-800-232-4636 or visit their website.
